title: Clarity
author: Nick Hart
summary: This is the first of Nick Hart's six-part series adapting Richard Claydon's work on leadership rituals into 'sense making disciplines' for school leaders. Hart's premise is that when leaders do not explicitly perform stabilising work, it reappears elsewhere as overload, friction and drift. Clarity, the first discipline, is produced through repeated and visible acts of judgement that reduce ambiguity about direction, priority and responsibility, even when uncertainty cannot be removed. He sets out four strategies: naming and ranking priorities, establishing direction before detail, making non-priorities explicit, and ending discussions with named ownership. Each is paired with concrete practices, and he argues these strategies do 'upstream' work that stops judgement and prioritisation drifting down to teams by default. He closes by framing the strategies as short, repeatable leader prompts for moments of overload, urgency or disagreement rather than as agenda items.
points: Hart borrows Claydon's claim that team flexibility comes from disciplined repetition, arguing that stabilising work left undone by leaders resurfaces as overload, friction and drift.
Ranking priorities, not merely listing them, gives teams a shared reference point; unranked priorities lead people to build their own hierarchy and fuel quiet competition between initiatives.
Explicitly naming what is not being pursued protects attention and legitimises refusal, turning 'not now' into shared judgement rather than individual failure.
Clarity is distinguished from certainty: it means creating enough shared understanding for collective action, closed off by making clear who owns the next step and when it will be reviewed.
quotes: Rather than working with the language of rituals and flexibility, I’m framing the same stabilising function as sense making disciplines and seeking to apply Richard’s insights to school leadership, shaping how we pay attention, interpret problems and coordinate the work so that it can proceed intelligently in complex conditions. What I’m taking from Richard’s work is not the metaphor but the underlying claim that when stabilising work is not done explicitly by leaders, it reappears elsewhere as overload, friction and drift.

Clarity is produced through deliberate acts of judgement, exercised repeatedly and made visible to others. In complex systems, leaders cannot eliminate uncertainty but they can reduce ambiguity about direction, priority and responsibility.
Where priorities are unranked, teams (and individuals) create their own hierarchy implicitly. This often leads to quiet competition between initiatives and uneven workload distribution.
When detail arrives before direction, teams tend to optimise locally. Decisions make sense in isolation but pull the system in different directions.

When this strategy is absent, overload accumulates quietly. People attempt to carry everything, often compensating through longer hours or reduced quality. Making non-priorities explicit turns absence into shared judgement rather than individual failure.
Without this move, sense making remains abstract. Energy dissipates between meetings and progress relies on individual initiative rather than collective coordination.
When leaders hold this work explicitly, others are freed to focus on execution rather than interpretation. Clarity and certainty are not the same.
